'''James Franklin Gibbons''' (born September 19, 1931) is an American electrical engineer and [[Academic administration|academic administrator]]. He is credited (together with [[w:William Shockley|William Shockley]]) with starting the semiconductor device fabrication laboratory at [[Stanford University]] that enabled the semiconductor industry and created [[Silicon Valley]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Where is the birthplace of Silicon Valley? Event aims to put the . |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2018/08/08/mountain-view-where-is-the-birthplace-of-silicon-valley/ |website=Mercury News |date=August 8, 2018 |access-date=3 November 2018}}</ref>

Gibbons is also credited for inventing Tutored Video Instruction, which is widely used at Stanford University and its Stanford Instructional Television Network. The Tutored Video Instruction is used to educate engineers and non students who are in need via SERA Learning Technologies (which Gibbons founded).<ref name="SU_TVI">{{cite web
|url= https://news.stanford.edu/news/1999/april28/gibbons-428.html
|title= Video lessons may help cool kids' rage
|author= Kathleen O'Toole
|date= April 28, 1999
|publisher= Stanford University
}}</ref>

Gibbons was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1974 for leadership as a teacher, author, and researcher in semiconductor electronics.

==Early life==
James F. Gibbons was born in Leavenworth, Kansas<ref name="JFG_OralHist" /> on September 19, 1931, to Clifford and Mary Gibbons. His father was a guard at United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, until Gibbons was about eight years old.<ref name="JFG_OralHist" />  At that time, his father was transferred to a minimum security prison in Texarkana, Texas.<ref name="JFG_OralHist" />  Gibbons spent his middle and high school years there, until he went off to college.<ref name="JFG_OralHist" />

==Higher education==
Gibbons left Texas to pursue his undergraduate degree in [[electrical engineering]] at [[Northwestern University]] chosen due to receiving a partial scholarship from Northwestern, Northwestern's proximity to Chicago and the jazz music scene there (Gibbons played trombone and was also pondering a possible musical career),<ref name="JFG_OralHist2">{{cite web
|url= http://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2013/12/102746628-05-01-acc.pdf
|title= Oral History of James F. "Jim" Gibbons
|author= Harry Sello
|date= November 16, 2012
|publisher= Computer History Museum
}}</ref> and also due to Northwestern's co-op requirement.<ref name="JFG_OralHist" />  Gibbons co-oped at Tungstal, where he worked on vacuum tubes being used in televisions.<ref name="JFG_OralHist" />  In 1953, after five years (due to the mandatory co-op), Gibbons finished his B.S. degree in electrical engineering at Northwestern University in 1953.<ref name="JFG_OralHist">{{cite web
|url= http://ethw.org/Oral-History:James_Gibbons
|title= An Oral History of James F. Gibbons
|author= David Morton
|date= May 31, 2000
|publisher= IEEE History Center
}}</ref>  He also earned a National Science Foundation fellowship from his efforts at Northwestern, which was able to be used at any school across the United States.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />

After discussions with his Northwestern advisor (who was the chairman of Electrical Engineering Department), Gibbons chose to accept admission to Stanford University for his advanced degree work.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  At Stanford, Gibbons took a course titled "Transistors and Active Circuit Design.”, which was being taught by [[w:John G. Linvill|John Linvill]], formerly of Bell Labs.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  This course captivated Gibbons and he spent extra time with Linvill, leading Linvill to convince Gibbons that he should stay at Stanford and earn a Ph.D.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  Gibbons did just that (graduating with a Ph.D. from Stanford in 1956<ref name="JFG_OralHist"/>) and his Ph.D. thesis was on a methodology for transistor circuit design that would utilize feedback to mitigate the variations between transistors of that time.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  Based on his efforts at Stanford, Gibbons was awarded a [[w:Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] scholarship, which he utilized at Cambridge University to work on grain boundaries in magnetic materials.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />

==Academic career==
After completing his work at Cambridge, Gibbons was considering several job opportunities when [[w:John G. Linvill|John Linvill]] again interceded.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  Linvill convinced Gibbons to consider a hybrid position where he would work 50% at [[w:Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory|Shockley Semiconductor]] to learn semiconductor fabrication techniques from [[w:William Shockley|William Shockley]] and the other 50% as an assistant professor at Stanford, setting up a laboratory to fabricate semiconductors and teaching the techniques to Stanford Ph.D. students.

On August 1, 1957, Gibbons joined the Stanford faculty<ref name="pyda">{{cite journal |title=In Brief |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.2813723 |journal=Physics Today |year=1985 |volume=38 |issue=1 |page=110 |doi=10.1063/1.2813723 |bibcode=1985PhT....38a.110. |access-date=3 November 2018|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and began his work with Shockley.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  Six months later, Gibbons' lab at Stanford produced its first silicon device.<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />  After presenting a conference paper on their results, the Stanford semiconductor fabrication lab became the cornerstone upon which [[w:John G. Linvill|John Linvill]] and Stanford built a solid-state electronics laboratory and attracted to Stanford some of the leading people in the burgeoning field of semiconductors, including persons such as [[w:Gerald Pearson|Gerald Pearson]] and [[w:John L. Moll|John Moll]].<ref name="JFG_OralHist2" />

Stanford named Gibbons as a professor of Electrical Engineering in 1964<ref name="JFG_SUHist">{{cite web
|url= https://engineering.stanford.edu/about/history
|title= History of the School of Engineering
|date= 2016-04-26
|publisher= Stanford University
}}</ref> and dean of the School of Engineering in 1984,<ref name="SU_PR1">{{cite web
|url= https://web.stanford.edu/dept/news/pr/95/950308Arc5341.html
|title= Engineering dean to take on new industrial relations role
|date= March 8, 1995
|publisher= Stanford University News Service
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160614055023/http://web.stanford.edu/dept/news/pr/95/950308Arc5341.html
|archive-date= June 14, 2016
|url-status= dead
}}</ref> a position he held until June 1996.<ref name="JFG_SUHist" />  In 1995, Gibbons was appointed as special counsel to the Stanford University President and Provost for Industry Relations at Stanford University.<ref name="SU_PR1" />

Gibbons also contributed to the Stanford Instructional Television Network; he invented a widely used Tutored Video Instruction<ref>{{cite news |title=Technology |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/12/15/archives/technology-dissatisfaction-as-a-spur-to-career.html |work=New York Times |date=December 15, 1976 |access-date=6 November 2018|last1=McElreny |first1=Victor K. }}</ref> that is used at Stanford University and in other places. This video network is to extend the education of engineers. Gibbon's Tutored video instruction has been used to educate the children of migrant farm workers and to help at-risk teens with their anger problems. He founded SERA Learning Technologies which utilizes this technology for that aim.<ref name="SU_TVI"/>

==Industry leadership==
He served on the Board of Directors of:

* SRI International
* Raychem
* Cisco Systems
* Lockheed-Martin

He also served on committees advising the Presidential Science Advisor in the Nixon, Reagan, Bush and Clinton administrations.

==Awards and honors==
Gibbons has received many awards and was elected a member of the American Academy or Arts and Sciences, the National Academy of Sciences, the [[National Academy of Engineering]], and as a Fellow of the IEEE.<ref name="SU_Profile">{{cite web
|url= https://profiles.stanford.edu/James-gibbons
|title= James F Gibbons, Professor (Research) of Electrical Engineering, Emeritus
|publisher= Stanford University
|access-date= November 5, 2018
|archive-date= June 16, 2020
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200616025115/https://profiles.stanford.edu/james-gibbons
|url-status= dead
}}</ref>

* He was awarded the IEEE Jack A. Morton Award in 1980 for his outstanding contributions in the field of solid-state devices.<ref name="IEEE_CLAW">{{cite web
|url= https://www.ieee.org/about/awards/awards_search.pdf
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140801084516/http://www.ieee.org/about/awards/awards_search.pdf
|url-status= dead
|archive-date= August 1, 2014
|title= Complete list of IEEE-Level Award Recipients and Citations
|website= [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE)
}}</ref>
* He was awarded the [[w:IEEE James H. Mulligan Jr. Education Medal|IEEE James H. Mulligan, Jr. Education Medal (formerly the IEEE Education Medal)]] in 1985 for his contributions to the vitality, imagination, and leadership of the members of the engineering profession.<ref>{{cite web
|url= https://www.ieee.org/documents/education_rl.pdf
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100619220444/http://ieee.org/documents/education_rl.pdf
|url-status= dead
|archive-date= June 19, 2010
|title= Complete list of IEEE James H. Mulligan, Jr. Education Medal recipients (PDF, 96 KB)
|website= [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE)
}}</ref>
* He was awarded the [[w:IEEE Founders Medal|IEEE Founders Medal]] in 2011 for his outstanding contributions to the leadership, planning, and administration of affairs of great value to the electrical and electronics engineering profession.<ref name="IEEE_CLAW" />
* He was awarded the Millennium Medal by the IEEE Electron Devices Society for his outstanding contributions.<ref>{{cite web
|url= http://eds.ieee.org/eds-millennium-medal-winners.html
|title= List of IEEE Millennium Medal Recipients
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150913015417/http://eds.ieee.org/eds-millennium-medal-winners.html
|archive-date= September 13, 2015
|url-status= dead
}}</ref>
* He was awarded the [[IEEE Paul Rappaport Award|Paul Rappaport Award]] by the IEEE Electron Devices Society in 1989 for co-authoring "Bandgap and Transport Properties of Si1-xGex by Analysis of Nearly Ideal Si/Si1-xGex/Si Heterojunction Bipolar Transistors T-ED/ED-36/10".<ref>{{cite web
|url= http://eds.ieee.org/paul-rappaport-award.html
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20101031193545/http://eds.ieee.org/paul-rappaport-award.html
|url-status= dead
|archive-date= October 31, 2010
|title= List of Paul Rappaport Award Recipients
}}</ref>
